analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal pay enforcement, bans employers from asking salary history, and protects workers who share wage information.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 201 cosponsors in the House but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten the federal equal pay law. Employers would have to prove that any pay gap between men and women doing the same job is truly job-related and necessary, and they could no longer lean on a broad defense that pay differences come from 'any factor other than sex.' Workers could recover compensatory and punitive damages and join class actions. Employers could not fire or punish workers for asking about or sharing wages, and could not demand a worker's past salary to set a new lower one. It would also require the EEOC to collect pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin, and it would direct the Labor Department to run pay-equity training and research.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and other workers paid less than male colleagues doing comparable work. It also protects job applicants: employers could no longer ask about salary history, a practice that lets earlier discrimination follow a worker from job to job. Workers who discuss wages would be shielded from retaliation, which helps pay gaps surface in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the employer defense to sex-based pay differences to factors that are job-related, consistent with business necessity, and account for the entire pay gap, with a carve-out when a less discriminatory alternative practice exists [S3].
Adds compensatory and punitive damages for equal pay violations, allows class actions to enforce equal pay claims, and lets the Labor Secretary bring enforcement including damages [S3].

Makes it unlawful to require workers to sign contracts or waivers barring them from sharing wage information, and strengthens retaliation protections for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages [S2,S3].
Bans employers from seeking or relying on a job applicant's wage history to set pay, with civil penalties up to $10,000 and damages for affected applicants [S3].
Directs the EEOC to issue regulations collecting compensation and employment data disaggregated by sex, race, and national origin, for use in enforcing pay discrimination laws [S2,S3].
Authorizes $15 million for grant-funded negotiation-skills training for girls and women, Department of Labor studies, outreach, and technical assistance to help small businesses comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially larger ones. They would face higher liability (compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, expanded penalties), new pay-data reporting to the EEOC, and for federal contractors an OFCCP compensation survey. Small businesses that are already exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act would be exempt from this bill too.

drawbacks.text: The damages and class-action provisions would raise litigation risk for employers, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some of that cost lands on businesses rather than directly on workers' paychecks [S3].

Narrowing the 'bona fide factor' defense means courts, not just employers, would have more say over whether market-driven pay differences pass the job-related and business-necessity tests, which businesses argued makes merit-based pay harder to defend [S2,S3].
The EEOC pay-data reporting requirement and the OFCCP contractor survey would add compliance and paperwork costs, which the bill itself instructs the EEOC to weigh against enforcement benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers genuinely stronger tools against pay discrimination: a weaker employer defense, real damages, protection for wage discussions, and a ban on salary-history questions that carry earlier discrimination forward. The costs are real but mostly compliance and litigation risk for employers, not something that would undo the pay gains for workers; the small-business exemption and technical assistance blunt the burden on the smallest firms. The design is fairly straightforward and the costs, on the whole, are the point: employers who currently get away with unexplained pay gaps would either fix them or pay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 4, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1,S5].
Its only action was that referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history [S5].
It carried 201 cosponsors, 200 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
Republicans held the House majority in the 115th Congress, which controlled the committee's agenda and the floor schedule.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new liability, pay-data reporting, and damages come out ahead because the bill never advanced. House Republicans who never acted on it also avoided casting a recorded vote on it.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act in the House on April 4, 2017.

for.name: 200 House Democrats (and 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including House Democratic leaders Nancy Pelosi and Steny Hoyer among the original sponsors [S3,S4].

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup, so the committee took no action. The record shows no committee action after referral [S5].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda and brought no equal pay legislation of this kind to the floor during the two-year Congress; the bill sat in committee its entire life [S5].

against.name: Business and employer groups (including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.role: Opponents of the Paycheck Fairness Act
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act in this and prior Congresses, arguing it would expose employers to unlimited damages and make merit-based pay decisions easier to challenge in court.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 200 of the 201 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans controlling the House, the bill never received any vote.

industries.note: They would face compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and expanded penalties for sex-based pay gaps, plus new EEOC pay-data reporting broken down by sex, race, and national origin [S3]. What they lose is the ability to keep unexplained pay differences off the books, which is money that would flow to workers [S3].

industries.industry: Employers that use salary history in hiring
industries.note: The bill bans seeking or relying on an applicant's wage history, with penalties up to $10,000 per offense. This practice can permanently depress the pay of workers whose earlier wages were set too low, so ending it protects job-hoppers and workers reentering the workforce [S3].

The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs would have to run a compensation-data survey covering at least half of nonconstruction contractor establishments each year and use it to target enforcement [S3].
